summary: Ezekiel 44 (31 verses) continues the story of glory. Starting with 'Then he brought me back by the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looks toward the east; and it was shut.', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Then he brought me back by the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looks toward the east; and it was shut.
“They shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister to me, and they shall keep my instruction.
The priests shall not eat of anything that dies of itself or is torn, whether it is bird or animal.

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 44?
questions.answer: In 31 verses, this chapter ezekiel 44 (31 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with 'then he brought me back by the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which looks toward the east; and it was shut.', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 44 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of glory. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 15 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: '“‘“But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who performed the duty of my sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from me, shall come near to me to minister to me. Th...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
